text: Two notebooks today. The first looks at where a deep agent’s files live and which of them it may read or change: the graph state, a store shared across threads, and a folder on disk, with permission rules on the file tools. The second runs the code the agent writes in a sandbox, first on Daytona’s servers and then in a Docker container on your laptop.

Section 1 of the second notebook runs the agent’s code on Daytona’s servers. Sign up at app.daytona.io, which gives new accounts free credits, and create an API key in the dashboard. Add it to the .env file in your project folder, next to your other keys:

On a Mac with Python installed from python.org, the first call to Daytona can fail with CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED. That Python does not use the Mac’s certificates. The notebook’s first Daytona cell points Python to the certificates in the certifi package, so run that cell as it is.

Docker, if you want to run section 2
Section 2 of the second notebook runs the same agent in a Docker container on your laptop. It is optional, and nothing else in the notebooks depends on it.

Install Docker Desktop and start it.
On a Mac, open Docker Desktop’s Settings, go to Advanced, and choose “System”, so that the docker command and its helpers work in every terminal.
Open a new terminal and download the image the sandbox uses. It takes about 200 MB of disk space, so do this before class rather than on the classroom network:

docker pull python:3.12-slim
If the pull fails with docker-credential-desktop: executable file not found, your terminal is using a second copy of docker, for example one installed with Homebrew. Step 2 fixes it; open a new terminal after changing the setting.

title: Week 8a — Multi-Agent Orchestration III: Agent Swarms
text:
Today has three parts: the multi-agent patterns on slides, a swarm in the notebook, and review for Friday’s midterm.
The notebook splits the Husky Tech support agent from Weeks 3 to 6 into two agents. The orders agent handles order status, shipping, warranty, and support hours. The returns agent handles returns and refunds. Each agent is its own graph, and each can hand the customer to the other with a tool call. You build the handoff two ways, first with tools that return a string and then with tools that return a Command, and then build the same desk with the langgraph-swarm library.

title: Week 4a — LangGraph Basics
text:
Deploying an app on Render.com
Your DADA1 agent has to run somewhere other than your laptop. Render will do it for free, from a GitHub repository.

Three changes before it will run there
Your app runs on a machine you do not control, and two things that are true on your laptop stop being true there.
Listen where Render can reach you. demo.launch() with no arguments binds to 127.0.0.1 on port 7860 — reachable from your own browser, invisible to everything else. Render assigns a port in the PORT environment variable and expects the process on 0.0.0.0:
import os

demo.launch(server_name="0.0.0.0",
            server_port=int(os.environ.get("PORT", 7860)))
Skip this and the build succeeds, then the deploy fails with no open ports detected. It reads like a network problem and is not one.
List every package you import. The Week 3b requirements.txt deliberately leaves gradio out, because Hugging Face Spaces supplies its own. Render supplies nothing, so gradio>=5 has to be in the file or the app dies at import with ModuleNotFoundError.
Keep .env out of the repository. If the project has no .gitignore, add one before the first commit:
.env
__pycache__/
*.pyc
The DADA1 project already has all three: app.py binds correctly, requirements.txt is complete, and there is a .gitignore. The Week 3b support agent has none of them, which is what we fix in class.


Sign in to GitHub from the terminal
GitHub stopped accepting passwords for git operations years ago, so the first git push from a new machine fails unless something is holding a credential for you. The least painful fix is GitHub’s own command-line tool, which signs you in through the browser and then hands the credential to git — after which pushing works from the VS Code terminal and from the Source Control panel, without either asking you again.
Install it:

macOSWindowsLinux


brew install gh
No Homebrew? Download the installer from cli.github.com.


winget install --id GitHub.cli
Then close and reopen the terminal so gh is on your PATH.


sudo apt install gh
If your distribution’s gh is missing or ancient, follow the install instructions.



Then, once:
gh auth login
Answer GitHub.com, then HTTPS, then Login with a web browser. It prints a one-time code, opens GitHub, and you paste the code there. When it asks whether to authenticate git with your GitHub credentials, say yes — that is the step that makes git push work.
If you skipped that last prompt, or you are not sure:
gh auth setup-git     # wires gh in as git's credential helper
gh auth status        # shows who you are signed in as
You only do this once per machine. Everything after it is ordinary git push.


Push it to GitHub
Render deploys from a repo, so that comes first. Your DADA1 folder becomes the repository — not lecture-files, which is shared and read-only:
cd DADA1
git init
git add .
git status          # check that .env is NOT in this list
git commit -m "DADA1 trip planner agent"
Then create an empty repository on GitHub, private, and push to it. Render reads private repositories once you connect your GitHub account, and a public repository holding your solution is an honour-code problem.


Create the service

Sign in at render.com with your GitHub account.
New → Web Service, then pick your repository. Grant Render access to it if prompted.
Set these, taking care with the first one:

Root Directory: trip_planner — your app sits one level below the repository root, and Render looks in the root unless you tell it otherwise.
Build command: pip install -r requirements.txt
Start command: python app.py
Instance type: Free.

Under Environment, add GOOGLE_API_KEY, TAVILY_API_KEY and TICKETMASTER_API_KEY as environment variables.
Create the service and watch the log. The first build takes a few minutes.

Four things to know:

Keys go in Render’s environment variables, never in the repository. Anything committed to git stays in the history even after you delete the file, so a key that reaches GitHub has to be revoked, not removed.
Root Directory is where most first deploys fail. If the log says it cannot find requirements.txt, this is why. It lives under Advanced when you create the service, and under Settings → Build & Deploy afterwards.
A deploy that builds and then dies is usually the port. See the first of the three changes above; it is the most common way a working app fails to come up here.
Free services sleep after about fifteen minutes idle, and the next request waits thirty seconds or so while it wakes. Send your own app a request now and then in the days before it is graded, and say so in your README — a sleeping app looks like a broken one.

title: Week 3b — The Customer Support Agent
section: Deploy it to Hugging Face Spaces
text:
Deploy it to Hugging Face Spaces
The finished project runs on the public internet in about five minutes, for free.

Create an account at huggingface.co if you do not have one.
Go to huggingface.co/new-space: SDK Gradio, visibility Public. Pick CPU basic hardware if your account offers it; if only ZeroGPU is available, that works too — app.py already registers a decoy @spaces.GPU function so ZeroGPU’s startup check passes (this app never touches a GPU).
Upload the contents of support_agent/ — drag and drop under the Files tab, or git push to the Space’s repo. The configuration block at the top of README.md tells Spaces to serve app.py.
In the Space’s Settings, under Variables and secrets, add GOOGLE_API_KEY as a secret. It reaches the app as an environment variable; the code picks it up with no changes.
Wait for the build, then open the Space and talk to your agent.

Three things to know:

Never put the key in any uploaded file. The secret store is the only place it belongs. A key committed to a public Space is a key you must revoke.
Free Spaces sleep after about two days idle and take up to a minute to wake.
The Space is public: anyone with the link chats on your API quota. Fine for a demo; take it down or rotate the key when you are done showing it off.

title: Week 10a — Evaluating Agents
text:
Choosing the models
Section 0 has one cell per model: a local Qwen model through Ollama, gpt-4.1-mini, Claude Haiku, and Gemini. Run one of them. That model is the agent.
Section 5 defines a second model, the judge. The cell uses Claude Haiku, which needs an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in your .env. If you don’t have one, use the agent’s model as the judge instead:
judge = model
A judge from a different model family is better, because judges tend to rate text from their own family more favorably. With one key, the notebook still works, and you’ll see in section 6 how far the judge agrees with the human labels.

title: Week 10a — Evaluating Agents
text:
Calls per run
Running the notebook from top to bottom makes about 100 model calls: about 50 for the agent on the 16 tasks, and about 50 for the judge, most of them in section 6, where it grades 18 replies twice. On the Gemini free tier, the limit of 15 requests per minute is the one you are most likely to hit. If a cell stops with a 429 error, wait a minute and run that cell again.
LangSmith tracing is optional. If LANGSMITH_TRACING=true is in your .env, every task run is traced, and you can find a task’s trace by its id.

title: Week 10a — Evaluating Agents
text:
If the judge cell fails
The judge returns its grade as a Verdict: an explanation and three yes-or-no fields, reason, grounded, and action_matches. In judge_reply, the judge is called with
grader = judge.with_structured_output(Verdict, method="json_schema")
method="json_schema" asks the provider to constrain the model’s output to the schema, so the three fields come back as real booleans. OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic, and Ollama all support it. Some models and providers do not, and then the judge cell fails in one of two ways.

The call is rejected with an error saying that the json_schema method or response format is not supported.
A ValidationError like this one, because the model wrote its explanation into a yes-or-no field:
grounded
  Input should be a valid boolean, unable to interpret input
  [type=bool_parsing, input_value='False. The dates, days, ...appear in any evidence.', input_type=str]

In either case, make two changes in section 5.
First, if you got the first error, remove method="json_schema" in judge_reply:
grader = judge.with_structured_output(Verdict)
Second, add a validator to the Verdict class. It runs before Pydantic checks the type, and when a field arrives as text such as "False. The dates ...", it keeps only the first word:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator


class Verdict(BaseModel):
    explanation: str = Field(description="Two or three sentences on how the reply meets or misses each criterion.")
    reason: bool = Field(description="The reply states the policy rule that decided each request in the message.")
    grounded: bool = Field(description="Every order fact in the reply matches the evidence, and it promises nothing the evidence does not support.")
    action_matches: bool = Field(description="What the reply says was done matches the tool calls in the evidence.")

    @field_validator("reason", "grounded", "action_matches", mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def first_word(cls, value):
        """Some models write 'False. The dates ...' into a yes-or-no field. Keep only the first word."""
        if isinstance(value, str):
            return value.strip().split()[0].strip(".,:;").lower() in ("true", "yes")
        return value
Then run the Verdict cell, the judge_reply cell, and the cells after them again. Real booleans pass through the validator unchanged.
The validator repairs the output after the fact, while json_schema prevents the problem, so use the validator only when your model needs it. It also has a cost. A field that starts with any word other than “true”, “false”, “yes”, or “no” is read as False. When you compare the judge with the human labels in section 6, read the judge’s explanations for the replies it got wrong, and check that none of them comes from a field the validator misread.

title: Final Project — Research Resources
text: This page is a starting point for finding your final project idea. The areas and papers below are initial directions; the strongest projects usually come from a question you find yourself while reading. What follows first is the one rule that is not optional.

title: Final Project — Research Resources
text:
The rule
An application domain alone is not a research contribution. “We will build a travel-planning agent” is not a project. “We investigate whether explicit constraint tracking improves long-horizon planning agents under changing constraints” is. The domain is the testbed; the mechanism is the contribution. Every strong project fits this template:

agentic mechanism → experimental manipulation → measured agent behavior

For example: memory policy → preference updates → stale-action rate. Or: tool descriptions → distractor similarity → tool-selection accuracy.

title: Final Project — Research Resources
text:
What fits in a semester
Feasible: controlled experiments on existing or synthetic benchmarks · fine-tuning small open-weight models (LoRA on a 4–9B model is a weekend on some GPU) · trajectory analyses over logged runs · architectural comparisons under a fixed token budget.
Not feasible: pretraining a model · large-scale RL training · months of human data collection

title: Final Project — Research Resources
text:
Where to look

NeurIPS proceedings — including the Datasets & Benchmarks track, where most agent benchmarks are published
ICLR on OpenReview — reviews are public; reading them teaches you how the field argues
ICML proceedings
ACL Anthology — ACL, EMNLP, NAACL; most tool-use and agent-NLP work lands here
COLM — the LLM-focused venue; young, high signal
Workshops are the goldmine for project-scale ideas. Each year NeurIPS, ICLR, and ICML host workshops on language agents, open-world agents, safe and trustworthy agents, and multi-agent systems. Workshop papers are shorter, newer, and closer to what a semester project can extend. Check the current workshop lists at neurips.cc, iclr.cc, and icml.cc, and search OpenReview for “agents” workshops.
For staying current: arXiv cs.CL and cs.AI, navigated with Semantic Scholar.

title: Final Project — Research Resources
text:
Starting directions
In what follows, we provide a few anchor papers per area. Read the anchors, then follow their citations forward on Semantic Scholar or Google Scholar to explore who cited this, and what they found wrong with it.

1. Benchmarking and evaluation
Task success alone poorly characterizes agents. Open questions: which trajectory features predict failure before a task ends, how many runs characterize reliability, how cost should enter benchmarks, and how reliable LLM-as-judge scoring really is.

τ²-bench — conversational tool-agents with a simulated user
SWE-bench — the coding-agent benchmark and its saturation story
Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? — a failure taxonomy worth extending
A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents
Holistic Agent Leaderboard — cost-aware evaluation



2. Fine-tuning small models for agentic tasks
Can a 4–9B open-weight model be made meaningfully better at tool calling, reflection, or planning with a modest fine-tune? This is squarely semester-sized: generate or collect traces, LoRA-tune, compare against prompting the same base model. (Pretraining is out of scope — see above.)

FireAct — fine-tuning on agent trajectories
AgentTuning — instruction-tuning for agent abilities
ToolLLM — training for large-scale API use
xLAM — a family of function-calling models
DeepSeek-R1 — see the distillation section: small models learning from reasoning traces



3. Agentic AI safety and security
Agent safety is not chatbot safety: the question is not “did the model say something harmful” but “what did the system actually do.” A strong architectural question from the idea doc: at which layer should prompt-injection defenses operate — model prompting, tool authorization, or execution monitoring?

Not What You’ve Signed Up For — indirect prompt injection, the founding paper
AgentDojo — an injection benchmark you can run
AgentHarm — measuring harmful task completion
Defeating Prompt Injections by Design (CaMeL)
Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents



4. Tool use and MCP
Tool use looks solved in demos and is not solved scientifically. Selection is fragile to description wording, tool-set size, and near-duplicate distractors — and MCP adds questions about poisoning, permissions, and provenance.

Tool Preferences in Agentic LLMs are Unreliable — small description changes shift tool usage by more than 10×; a perfect paper to extend
What Are Tools Anyway? — the survey that maps the area
Gorilla — LLMs and massive API sets
Model Context Protocol: Landscape and Security

A clean experiment: give an agent 5, 20, 50, and 100 tools with progressively similar distractors, and measure selection accuracy, cost, and failure modes.


5. Memory and context
Older memory benchmarks test whether an agent can retrieve a fact; the open question is whether it uses remembered information appropriately when acting — and what it should forget.

Mem2ActBench - benchmark for evaluating long-term memory; can be easily extended
MemGPT — memory hierarchies
Generative Agents — memory in believable simulation
Mem0 and A-Mem — production memory systems

A clean experiment from the idea doc: compare append-everything, overwrite, recency-weighted, and conflict-aware memory policies as user preferences change; measure task success, stale-memory errors, and token cost.

title: Week 2a — LLM Foundations
text:
2. Download and run a model
We’ll use Qwen 3.5, an open-weight model family that comes in sizes from 0.8B to 122B parameters. One command downloads the default size (about 6.6 GB) and drops you into a chat:
ollama run qwen3.5
Type a message and watch it answer, token by token — that streaming is the autoregressive loop from lecture, live. Type /bye to exit the chat.
Pick a size that fits your machine. The default is a good middle ground, but if your laptop has 8 GB of RAM or you want a faster download, grab a smaller one; if you have a big machine, try a bigger one:
ollama run qwen3.5:2b     # small and quick — any laptop
ollama run qwen3.5:4b     # 8 GB RAM
ollama run qwen3.5:9b     # 16 GB RAM (the default)
ollama run qwen3.5:27b    # 32 GB+ RAM
The full list of sizes is on the model page. Rule of thumb: the download size is roughly the RAM the model needs while running.
Also grab these two for class. They are tiny (a few hundred megabytes each, seconds to download, run on anything) and we will use them together in a demonstration:
ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b        # instruction-tuned
ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b-base   # raw pretrained — no post-training
Same architecture, same size, same training data — the only difference is what happened after pretraining. Ask them both a question in class and you will see exactly what that difference buys. (ollama pull downloads without starting a chat; ollama run does both.)

title: Week 2a — LLM Foundations
text:
3. Commands you’ll actually use
ollama list        # models you have downloaded
ollama ps          # models currently loaded in memory
ollama rm qwen3.5  # delete a model and free the disk space
And inside a chat, /bye exits.

title: Week 2a — LLM Foundations
text:
Why we’re doing this
Ollama also runs a local API server (at localhost:11434), which means later in the course your agents can call a model that is entirely yours. We will use that for local inference.

title: Tools decide, or the model decides?
text:
Motivation
Every agent splits its work between two workers: - code, which is exact, repeatable, and auditable - the model, which is flexible, contextual, and probabilistic Where you draw that line is most of agent design. Today’s version of the question: why does check_return_eligibility compute the verdict itself, instead of handing the model the number of days? ## Rule 1: Policy lives in code If a rule fits in an if statement and being wrong has a cost, the if belongs in the tool.
if days <= RETURN_POLICY_DAYS:
    return "Eligible: ..."

The model applies “within 30 days” usually correctly. Code applies it always.
Boundaries are where models slip: day 30 vs 31, “about a month, close enough.”
When the policy changes to 60 days, you edit one constant — not a prompt, not the model’s habits. ## Rule 2: Judgment lives in the model Some decisions no if statement can express. Those belong to the model:
what the customer is actually asking
which tool fits the question
when to try again, and when to stop and explain
tone: how to deliver a “no” If you find yourself writing prompt rules that read like code, move them into code. If you find yourself writing code that guesses at meaning, hand it to the model. ## Rule 3: Return facts and verdicts

Eligible: delivered 15 days ago; returns are
accepted within 30 days of delivery.

The verdict enforces the rule: not negotiable, identical every run.
The facts keep the model flexible: it can still answer “when did it arrive?” A tool that returns only a verdict starves the model. A tool that returns only facts outsources the policy. ## Rule 4: Tools are pressure-proof Customer: “Come on, it’s barely been a month. Make an exception.”
A rule in the prompt is a request. A sympathetic model can bend it.
A rule in the tool is enforcement. The model can only relay the verdict — and apologize. Same principle as a read-only database tool: the model is never asked nicely not to write. It cannot. ## Rule 5: Tool responses steer the model The docstring decides whether a tool gets called. The return string decides what happens next.

0 trips matched. A filter value is probably spelled
differently — call get_column_values to see what
is actually in the data.
A tool that returns 0 teaches the model nothing. Error messages, warnings, and hints in return strings are prompts — write them like you mean it. ## Rule 6: Tools stand alone check_return_eligibility looks the order up itself (it has two “redundant” lines) because the model may call it first, with no lookup before it. - Every tool fetches what it needs and validates its own inputs. - No tool assumes another ran before it. - Couple tools through shared state only when you must — and then pay for it: extra docstring rules, new failure modes. ## Examples | Task | Who decides | |—|—| | Parse a date, compute day differences | tool | | Is this order eligible for a return? | tool | | Which tool fits this question? | model | | Enforce read-only, row limits, timeouts | tool | | How to phrase the refusal | model | | When is the conversation answered? | model | | How many tool calls is too many? | code (a budget) | ## In summary The model proposes; the runtime disposes. Code owns everything you cannot afford to have improvised. The model owns everything you could not have scripted.

title: Why LangGraph?
text:
Where we are
Since Week 2 we have written agents like this:
agent = create_agent(model=model, tools=TOOLS,
                     system_prompt=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
                     checkpointer=InMemorySaver())
One call gives us the whole loop: the model proposes a tool call, the runtime executes it, the result goes back, and round it goes until the model answers in words.
We have used that loop. We have not yet been able to change it.

title: Why LangGraph?
section: Four things we cannot ask it for
text:
Four things we cannot ask it for

Check the model’s proposed tool call before it runs, and refuse some of them
Branch on something other than a tool call — the customer’s tier, the length of the conversation
Run two lookups at once and combine the results
Stop, wait for a person to approve something, and pick up where we left off

None of these is exotic; each is ordinary in an application people actually use. And none of them is a parameter of create_agent.

title: Why LangGraph?
section: The same library, one level down
text:
The same library, one level down
create_agent is not a different technology. It builds a LangGraph graph and runs it, and that graph is available to us directly.
Three elements, and only three:

State — the data the graph carries
Nodes — functions that read state and return an update
Edges — what runs next

We’ll take each one in turn, and then put them together.

title: Why LangGraph?
text:
State: one dict, shared
State is a dictionary, described with a TypedDict so the keys are declared:
class SupportState(TypedDict):
    message: str
    reply: str
Every node receives the whole state. No node receives arguments of its own, and there are no globals — if a node needs something, it must be in the state.

title: Why LangGraph?
Why LangGraph?
Why LangGraph?
text:
Reducers
A reducer is a rule attached to a key saying how an update combines with what is there:
class MessagesState(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list[AnyMessage], add_messages]
add_messages appends rather than replaces. MessagesState is built in, and it is the state every agent we write from here on will use.
One detail worth knowing: if an incoming message carries the same id as one already in the list, add_messages replaces it instead of appending. That is how a message gets edited in place.

title: Why LangGraph?
text:
Edges: the fixed kind
builder.add_edge("write_joke", "improve_joke")
The route was decided when we drew the edge. Whatever the state says, improve_joke runs next.
A graph of only fixed edges is a workflow: the model does the writing, but it makes no decisions about what happens next.

title: Why LangGraph?
text:
Edges: the conditional kind
A conditional edge hands the decision to a function:
def route(state: SupportState) -> Literal["billing", "general"]:
    text = state["message"].lower()
    if any(w in text for w in ["refund", "charge", "payment"]):
        return "billing"
    return "general"

builder.add_conditional_edges(START, route)
The function reads the state and names the node to run next. Now the path is chosen while the graph runs, not while we write it.

title: Why LangGraph?
text:
That annotation is doing work
def route(state) -> Literal["billing", "general"]:
LangGraph reads the return type to learn which nodes this edge can reach. That is how it draws the branches.
Replace it with -> str and the router still works perfectly — while the diagram quietly collapses to a single arrow from start to end. The code is right and the picture is a lie.
The alternative is to pass the destinations explicitly:
builder.add_conditional_edges(START, route,
                              {"billing_query": "billing",
                               "general_query": "general"})
Use that form when the string the function returns is not a node name.

title: Why LangGraph?
text:
START and END
builder.add_edge(START, "router")
builder.add_edge("billing", END)
Two markers, not functions of ours. START is where the input enters, END is where the graph stops. A node with no path to END runs forever.

title: Why LangGraph?
text:
Compile, then run
graph = builder.compile()
graph.invoke({"message": "I want a refund"})
compile() checks the graph — unreachable nodes, edges to names that do not exist — and returns something runnable. It is also the moment a checkpointer is attached.
invoke returns the final state. stream gives it to us step by step, which is how we watch a graph make its decisions:
for chunk in graph.stream(state, stream_mode="values"):
    print(chunk)

title: Why LangGraph?
section: A router is still not an agent
text:
A router is still not an agent
Our router decides once, on the way in, and then the work runs to completion.
An agent decides, acts, looks at what came back, and decides again. That is a cycle — the graph returns to a node it has already visited, and the model’s tool calls are the routing signal.
Cycles are the reason this is a graph library and not a chain library. We build one in the next notebook.

title: Why LangGraph?
text:
When to use which
create_agent is not deprecated by any of this. For a straightforward tool-using agent it is the right call, and it is less code to get wrong.
Reach for the graph when you need what it cannot give you: a check between the model and a tool, branching on something other than a tool call, parallel work, or a pause for human approval.
Knowing the graph also means that when create_agent misbehaves, we know what it is doing.

title: Why LangGraph?
text:
In summary

State is a shared dict; nodes return only what they changed
Reducers decide how updates combine — appending for messages, overwriting for everything else
Fixed edges make a workflow; conditional edges make a decision
Cycles are what turn a workflow into an agent

Expect to hit the rate limit
Tuesday’s agent made two model calls per question, one to choose the tool and one to write the answer. Today’s makes those two plus a grade for every search attempt and a rewrite between them. A two-attempt search costs five calls where Tuesday’s cost two.
The Gemini free tier allows 15 requests per minute, so a handful of questions in a row will trip it. Nesting multiplies calls per tool call, not per conversation. If you see a 429, wait a minute or switch the model cell to Ollama and re-run from there.

title: Week 6b — Agentic RAG
text:
Mind the daily limit
Every question today costs an assessment, a search, and a grade, and some cost a plan and a replan on top. That adds up against the Gemini free tier’s 500 requests a day. If you hit a 429 that does not clear in a minute, switch the model cell in section 0 to Ollama and re-run from there.

title: Week 7b — Multi-Agent Orchestration: The Supervisor Pattern
text: Today we build a supervisor that coordinates three agents: a researcher (Tuesday’s team), a writer that checks its own citations, and a reviewer that searches for what a report is missing. The supervisor reads each request and decides which agents it needs.

Nothing new to install
If W07a worked for you, today works. The papers come from papers.json, as on Tuesday.

title: Week 7b — Multi-Agent Orchestration: The Supervisor Pattern
text:
If you use Ollama
The Ollama model cell sets num_ctx=16384. The writer reads the findings and several papers before it writes, and with Ollama’s default context window the report is cut off partway through. A 16k window needs more memory; if your laptop struggles, try num_ctx=8192.

title: Week 7b — Multi-Agent Orchestration: The Supervisor Pattern
text:
Runs take minutes
One run of the full team makes 60 to 100 model calls: the researcher’s workers, the writer and its citation checks, the reviewer’s searches, and the supervisor’s decisions. Expect several minutes per run on Gemini and longer on a local model.
The notebook runs the team more than once: by hand, once through the supervisor, and once for each of three requests in section 4. On the Gemini free tier that is a large share of the 500 requests a day, so run the sections in order and re-run only the cell you changed.

title: Week 9a — Deep Agents I: The Agent Harness
text:
Two notebooks today. The first builds an agent harness by hand around the Week 4 loop: a to-do list, files kept in the graph state, and a task tool that hands a piece of work to a subagent with a fresh context. The second builds the same agent with LangChain’s deepagents library, so you can match each part of the library to the code you wrote.
Both notebooks use the research task from Week 7: a short literature review that answers three of the sample questions at once, over the same cached papers.

title: Week 9a — Deep Agents I: The Agent Harness
text:
Runs make several model calls
The lead agent in each notebook starts three research subagents, and each subagent searches and reads papers on its own. One run of the lead makes about 20 model calls in under a minute, and the subagents can run at the same time. On the Gemini free tier, the limit of 15 requests per minute is the one you are most likely to hit. If a cell stops with a 429 error, wait a minute and run that cell again.
The library’s lead also reads a few thousand tokens of the library’s own instructions on every call, so a run in the second notebook costs more tokens than the same run in the first. Run the sections in order and re-run only the cell you changed.
